topic.subject: general
topic.title: Artificial intelligence basics
topic.scope: what AI is, learning from examples, chatbots can be wrong, bias in data, AI in daily apps, myths that AI thinks like a human

nodes.name: What AI is
Meaning of artificial intelligence
AI is software that does tasks like recognising, predicting or writing
Most AI is a program, not a robot body
Normal programs follow fixed rules; AI learns its rules from data
external_prereqs: what an algorithm or step-by-step instruction is

nodes.name: Learning from examples
Training with data
Many varied examples help an AI learn better
AI finds patterns in data; it does not understand meaning
Labelled examples tell the AI the right answer while training
external_prereqs: what a label or category is

nodes.name: Using a trained AI
A trained AI makes guesses on new inputs using learned patterns
Chatbots write by predicting likely next words
Limits of AI: mistakes and bias
Chatbots can be wrong
A confident-sounding answer is not necessarily correct
Chatbots can make up facts, names and sources
external_prereqs: what a source or reference is

nodes.name: Important answers should be checked with reliable sources
external_prereqs: what a reliable source is (textbook, government site)

nodes.name: Bias in data
Unrepresentative or prejudiced data gives unfair AI results
AI is not automatically neutral or perfect
AI in daily life and AI versus human thinking
AI in daily apps
Maps, voice assistants, spam filters and photo apps use AI
Recommendations are predictions from your past activity and others' data
external_prereqs: what an app account or history is

nodes.name: AI versus human thinking
AI has no feelings, wishes or awareness
Each AI is good only at the narrow task it was trained for
external_prereqs: what a task or skill is

misconceptions.statement: Artificial intelligence always means a robot that looks and walks like a human.
misconceptions.why: Films and cartoons usually show AI as humanoid robots.
misconceptions.fix: Most AI is software inside phones, websites and computers. It has no body at all, like the program that suggests videos or translates text.

probe.question: Is the spam filter in your email an example of AI?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it is not a robot.

misconceptions.root_belief: the popular picture of a thing is all of it

misconceptions.statement: Any program that runs on a computer is artificial intelligence.
misconceptions.why: Students hear 'smart' and 'AI' used for every digital gadget.
misconceptions.fix: A normal program only follows fixed steps written by a person, like a calculator. AI is different because it learns patterns from data.

probe.question: A calculator app always adds numbers using fixed rules. Is it AI?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is a computer program.

misconceptions.root_belief: everything in a broad group is the same kind

misconceptions.statement: Programmers type in the answer to every possible question before an AI is used.
misconceptions.why: Students think computers only repeat what people stored in them.
misconceptions.fix: Programmers do not write all answers. They give the AI many examples, and it learns patterns to answer new questions.

probe.question: How can an AI recognise a handwritten digit it has never seen before?
probe.wrong_answer: Programmers had already stored that exact digit in it.

misconceptions.root_belief: output must be stored in advance, not produced
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of students' ideas about machine learning and computers in school computing education

misconceptions.statement: Showing an AI thousands of examples of only one kind always makes it better at everything.
misconceptions.why: Students believe more data is always better, ignoring variety.
misconceptions.fix: The examples must be varied and cover the cases the AI will meet. Many photos of only one kind of cat will not help it recognise other animals.

probe.question: An AI is trained on 10,000 photos of only white cats. Will it recognise black cats well?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because 10,000 is a lot of photos.

misconceptions.root_belief: more of something always means better results
misconceptions.source_hint: research on training data representativeness in machine learning education

misconceptions.statement: If an AI gives a correct answer, it must understand the meaning like a person does.
misconceptions.why: Fluent, correct answers look like understanding.
misconceptions.fix: AI finds patterns in the data it was trained on. It can give right answers without knowing what the words or pictures mean.

probe.question: An AI labels a photo 'dog' correctly. Does it know what a dog is like we do?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it understands dogs just as we do.

misconceptions.root_belief: a correct output proves real understanding
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of children's and learners' anthropomorphic ideas about intelligent machines

misconceptions.statement: An AI can learn to recognise cats without anyone ever showing it examples.
misconceptions.why: Students think computers are born knowing things or learn by themselves like magic.
misconceptions.fix: An AI learns only from the data it is given, such as many photos marked 'cat' or 'not cat'. Without examples it learns nothing.

probe.question: Can an AI sort photos into 'cat' and 'dog' if it was never given any photos to learn from?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it will work it out by itself.

misconceptions.root_belief: knowledge appears without any input

misconceptions.statement: Once an AI is trained, its answers on new inputs are always correct.
misconceptions.why: Students treat computer output as exact like a calculator.
misconceptions.fix: A trained AI only makes a best guess from patterns, so it can be wrong, especially on cases unlike its training data.

probe.question: A trained face-unlock AI fails in dim light. Is that impossible for a trained AI?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a trained AI never makes mistakes.

misconceptions.root_belief: machines never make mistakes
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of learners' trust in algorithmic output

misconceptions.statement: A chatbot finds a ready-made answer on the internet and copies it out.
misconceptions.why: Students compare chatbots with search engines.
misconceptions.fix: A chatbot builds its reply by predicting which words are likely to come next, based on patterns it learned from lots of text. It does not just copy a stored answer.

probe.question: How does a chatbot produce a poem you asked for that nobody wrote before?
probe.wrong_answer: It searched and copied that poem from the internet.

misconceptions.root_belief: answers are always looked up, never produced

misconceptions.statement: If a chatbot sounds sure and writes neatly, its answer must be correct.
misconceptions.why: Fluent, confident language is how people usually recognise knowledgeable speakers.
misconceptions.fix: A chatbot can write wrong answers in a very confident tone. How sure it sounds says nothing about whether it is true.

probe.question: A chatbot confidently says Mumbai is the capital of India. Should you trust it because it sounds sure?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it sounds very sure so it must be right.

misconceptions.root_belief: sounding confident means being true
misconceptions.source_hint: research on trust and over-reliance on AI-generated text

misconceptions.statement: A chatbot never makes up facts or book names; it only says things that are true.
misconceptions.why: Students think a computer cannot lie or invent.
misconceptions.fix: Chatbots sometimes invent facts, names, quotes or sources that look real but do not exist. This is called hallucination.

probe.question: A chatbot gives you the title of a book and its author for your project. Is the book surely real?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, chatbots only give true information.

misconceptions.root_belief: machines only produce truth
misconceptions.source_hint: documented AI hallucination reports in language-model evaluations and media-literacy guidance

misconceptions.statement: If two different chatbots give the same answer, it must be correct.
misconceptions.why: Students think agreement between sources proves truth.
misconceptions.fix: Chatbots may have learned from similar data and repeat the same mistake. Check important facts in a textbook or an official government source.

probe.question: Two chatbots both say a wrong date for an event. Is the date verified?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, both agree so it is verified.

misconceptions.root_belief: agreement between sources means it is true

misconceptions.statement: AI trained on lots of data cannot be unfair because data is just facts.
misconceptions.why: Students think numbers and records are neutral.
misconceptions.fix: Data is collected by people and can leave out some groups or show old unfair habits. An AI learns those patterns and repeats the unfairness.

probe.question: A job-selection AI is trained on past hiring records that mostly chose men. Will it treat women fairly?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, data is only facts so it will be fair.

misconceptions.root_belief: data and numbers are neutral facts
misconceptions.source_hint: documented cases of biased hiring and face-recognition systems in algorithmic fairness research

misconceptions.statement: An AI is biased only when its programmer deliberately wants to be unfair.
misconceptions.why: Students think unfairness always needs a bad intention.
misconceptions.fix: Bias can appear by accident when the training data misses some groups or contains old prejudice, even if nobody meant harm.

probe.question: A voice AI understands boys' voices better because it was trained mostly on boys. Did a programmer plan this?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, someone must have wanted it to be unfair.

misconceptions.root_belief: unfair outcomes need a deliberate cause

misconceptions.statement: Computers have no opinions, so decisions by AI are always fairer than decisions by people.
misconceptions.why: Machines seem emotionless and so are assumed to be impartial.
misconceptions.fix: AI can copy the unfairness hidden in its data, so it is not automatically fair. People need to check its results.

probe.question: Should a school fully hand over scholarship choices to an AI because machines are fair?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a machine is always fair and has no bias.

misconceptions.root_belief: machines are neutral and cannot be wrong
misconceptions.source_hint: research on automation bias and perceived objectivity of algorithms

misconceptions.statement: An email spam filter works only from a fixed list of banned words that people typed in.
misconceptions.why: Students see simple rules they can imagine and miss the learning part.
misconceptions.fix: Modern spam filters learn from many emails marked as spam and not spam, and keep improving. They look at many patterns, not only a few words.

probe.question: How can a spam filter catch a new spam message with words never listed before?
probe.wrong_answer: It cannot; it only catches words from its fixed list.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from simple cases works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: AI is used only in big laboratories and space missions, not in everyday phone apps.
misconceptions.why: AI sounds advanced and distant from daily life.
misconceptions.fix: Everyday apps already use AI, such as maps predicting traffic, voice assistants, translation, photo sorting and video suggestions.

probe.question: Does a phone's voice assistant that understands your speech use AI?
probe.wrong_answer: No, AI is only in laboratories.

misconceptions.root_belief: advanced technology is far from daily life

misconceptions.statement: A video app shows the same recommended videos to every user.
misconceptions.why: Students think an app is one fixed list like a TV channel.
misconceptions.fix: Recommendations are predicted separately for each user from their watching history and what similar users liked, so two people see different videos.

probe.question: You and your friend open the same video app. Will you see the same recommended videos?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the app shows everyone the same list.

misconceptions.root_belief: everyone gets the same output from a system

misconceptions.statement: Whatever an app recommends is the best and most true choice for me.
misconceptions.why: Personalised suggestions feel like expert advice.
misconceptions.fix: Recommendations only predict what you may keep watching or buying from past data. They may be repetitive, miss better options or push you towards one kind of content.

probe.question: A shopping app recommends a product. Does that prove it is the best one for you?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the AI knows what is best for me.

misconceptions.root_belief: what is shown is the best or true choice

misconceptions.statement: A chatbot feels hurt or happy when you scold or praise it.
misconceptions.why: Chatbots speak in a friendly human way and say 'I feel'.
misconceptions.fix: A chatbot has no feelings or awareness. It produces words that look like feelings because it learned from human text.

probe.question: A chatbot writes 'I am sad you are leaving'. Does it really feel sad?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it feels sad like a person.

misconceptions.root_belief: speaking like people means feeling like people
misconceptions.source_hint: research on anthropomorphism of conversational agents and children's ideas about machine minds

misconceptions.statement: An AI that plays chess better than any person can also drive a car or write stories well.
misconceptions.why: Students think intelligence is one general ability that carries across tasks.
misconceptions.fix: Most AI is built and trained for one narrow job. A chess AI has not learned to drive or write.

probe.question: A champion chess AI is put in a car. Can it drive safely?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a clever AI can do any task.

misconceptions.root_belief: skill in one area carries over to all
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student conceptions of machine intelligence and narrow versus general AI

misconceptions.statement: Artificial intelligence means a machine that is as clever as a human in everything.
misconceptions.why: The word 'intelligence' is taken in its everyday human meaning.
misconceptions.fix: In everyday technology, AI means programs that do specific tasks, like recognising speech or predicting, by learning from data. They are not all-round human minds.

probe.question: Is a photo app that sorts pictures of faces AI, even though it cannot do anything else?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it is not as clever as a human.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: AI thinks and decides what it wants on its own, just like a human mind.
misconceptions.why: Films and news present AI as having its own will.
misconceptions.fix: AI has no wishes or goals of its own. It follows patterns learned from data and the goals people set for it.

probe.question: Can a chatbot decide by itself to start working on a goal that nobody gave it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it thinks and wants things like a person.

misconceptions.root_belief: anything that acts like us is like us
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of learners' anthropomorphic and science-fiction-influenced ideas about AI

misconceptions.statement: A chatbot always knows the latest news from today.
misconceptions.why: Students think it is connected live to everything on the internet.
misconceptions.fix: A chatbot learns from data collected up to a certain date, so it can miss recent events unless it is connected to a live search tool.

probe.question: Will a chatbot trained last year surely know yesterday's cricket match score?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it always knows the latest news.

misconceptions.root_belief: a tool knows everything up to this moment
